activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The coefficients in a balanced chemical equation give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses.
story:
The sub was late again, which meant the stoichiometry quiz would start without Ms. Hamdan and without anyone to answer questions, and Laurie sat at her lab station turning her pencil over and over the way she did when she wanted something in her hands to blame. Fanny had already written her name at the top of her paper in her looping cursive and was now writing something else, fast, with the confidence of someone who had not read the problem twice. Across the aisle, Alivia was reading the whiteboard with her chin propped on her fist, mouthing the numbers.

The problem on the board gave a mass of methane, four point eight grams, and asked for the mass of water produced in the reaction, whose balanced equation was written underneath with a 1 in front of the methane and a 2 in front of the water. Laurie had done the molar mass part the night before, in her room, with the textbook open and her phone face down, and she remembered the pleasant arithmetic of it, sixteen grams per mole for methane, eighteen for water, everything converting into everything else like currency. But somewhere between her room and this lab the logic had come apart, and now she stared at the equation and thought, well, one to two, so double the mass, and began to write nine point six grams.

She stopped with the pencil a centimeter off the paper. The night before, she had converted the four point eight grams into moles first, that was the whole point of molar mass, that it let you count particles you could never count. She had a sudden somatic memory of it, the way her shoulders had dropped when the units canceled, and she thought she might be on to something, though she could not yet say what.

"Nine point six," Fanny whispered across the aisle, holding up her paper. "One to two, right? You just double it."

Laurie looked at the equation. The coefficients sat there, small and certain, one and two, and she thought about what they were actually counting, not grams on a scale but the invisible packages the grams were converted into. The whole trick of the unit, the reason anyone bothered with molar mass at all, was that it turned mass into a count, and a count was the only thing a ratio of small whole numbers could honestly describe.

"I don't think it's the ratio of masses," she whispered back. "I think the coefficients give the ratio of moles. So you convert first, then use the one to two, then convert back."

Fanny stared at her. Alivia had turned around, chin still on her fist. "Say that again," Alivia said, and Laurie did, slower this time, tracing it on the air with her pencil: grams of methane into moles of methane, moles of methane times two over one, moles of water back into grams. When she did it on her scratch paper the answer came out under eleven grams, bigger than nine point six, which felt wrong until she saw why. A mole of water weighed more than a mole of methane. Mass was not the thing being doubled; the count was.

At the front of the room the door opened and Ms. Hamdan came in with her coat still on, apologizing to the sub, and Laurie felt a flash of something that was almost superstition, as though the teacher's arrival had been summoned by the problem solving itself. Ms. Hamdan began circulating. When she reached Fanny's paper she stopped, tapped the nine point six with one finger, and said nothing, which for Ms. Hamdan was a lecture. Fanny looked at the number, then at Laurie, then erased it so hard the paper thinned.

Here was the twist Laurie had not expected: when Ms. Hamdan reached Laurie's paper, she paused on the conversion line, and Laurie saw her own mistake before the teacher's finger found it. She had used thirty-two grams per mole for methane instead of sixteen, the mass of oxygen, a number she'd grabbed from a different column of her notes in a moment of confidence, and it had marched straight through the whole calculation, doubling everything downstream. She had the ratio right and the arithmetic wrong. She raised her hand, said, "I used the wrong molar mass on the first line," and Ms. Hamdan nodded once and moved on, and Laurie fixed it with her ears hot, aware that being right about one thing had made her sloppy about another.

After the papers were collected, Fanny leaned across the aisle. "So you can know the idea and still be a charlatan with the numbers," she said, and Laurie laughed, surprised, because Fanny had picked up the word from a documentary they'd watched in history class about a fake art dealer, and it fit, in its way. It also delimited something Laurie had been circling all week: the difference between understanding a principle and actually being able to carry it through, with no gaps, on paper, under time, while someone watched. She didn't yet know where she stood between those two things, and she suspected the distance was not something she could measure in moles.

The bell was minutes away. Alivia was copying the corrected version of the problem into her notebook, and Laurie pulled her stool over next to her and said, "Do it once more with a different mass, and I'll check you, and then you check me."

Alivia wrote 9.6 grams at the top of a fresh page and slid her calculator across the bench.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.
story:
The natatorium smelled of chlorine and cold concrete, and by the third week of the season Clara had learned to read the light that came through the high windows, how it moved across lane four by the end of practice and turned the water the color of an old coin. She was not the fastest on the team, but she had the discipline for the medley relay, and Mr. Oliveira had put her second, between Reagan's backstroke and Lydia's breaststroke, which meant she swam anchor in feeling if not in fact.

On Fridays the team did dryland on the deck, and today the coach had dragged out a thick rope and a padded sled. He explained it in his flat, unbothered way: one swimmer at a time would haul the sled the width of the deck, and then they would try it in groups of four, the way a tug of war works, and he would time them all. Clara went first alone. The rope bit into her palms and the sled screeched over the tile, and when she finished, breathless, the coach held up the stopwatch and said nothing, which from him was approval.

Then the groups. Clara pulled with Lydia, Reagan, and a senior whose name Clara still half-knew. They set their feet, the coach whistled, and they heaved. The sled moved. It just moved lazily, grudgingly, like something being asked a favor. Reagan swore. Lydia laughed the particular laugh she used to cover embarrassment, high and quick, and the coach stared at the watch, tapped it, and stared again.

"Again," he said.

They went again, and it was worse, and Clara stood there breathing with her hands on her knees while the coach wrote numbers in his small damp notebook. She had seen something like this before, in a psychology book her mother had left on the kitchen table over the summer, a book she had picked up mostly because the cover was the same green as the pool at night. She had read a paragraph about rope pulling, and now, watching Reagan shake out her arms and the senior check her palms for rope burn, the paragraph came back to her whole.

"French engineer," Clara said. "Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913. He found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone."

The coach looked up. "Where'd you get that?"

"A book. It was in this book my mom was reading." She felt awkward saying it, like admitting she read things by accident, but Reagan had turned around, and Lydia was frowning at the rope as if it had lied to her.

"So we're lazy together," Reagan said.

"No. I don't think that's it." Clara was not sure what it was; the book had not lingered on reasons, and she did not want to invent one. But the fact itself she trusted, because she was looking at it. She thought about the relay, about how she had swum her splits in practice, how much faster she went when she dove in alone against the clock than when she swam second in a line of four, how the water felt different when the team's noise faded behind the block. She had assumed that was tiredness, or nerves. Now she wasn't sure, and she said so.

That evening her mother drove her home through the rain, and Clara watched the wipers mesmerize their arc across the glass, back and forth, the same clean sweep every time, while she tried to hold two thoughts at once. One was that she loved the team, loved the specific warmth of it, Lydia saving her a seat, Reagan fixing her goggles strap without being asked, the way nobody had to explain anything to anybody. The other was that in groups, each of them pulled less, and it was almost axiomatic to her coach that the team made you better, an article of faith so settled it functioned as the team's whole zeitgeist, printed on the shirts, chanted in the showers. Both things seemed true. She could not make them into one clean rule, and she suspected the honest position was to stop trying.

At the next practice, the coach set up the sled again, but this time he draped a towel over the stopwatch, and he made them pull in a line where each rope ran separately to the sled, so that nobody could hide inside the group's effort and nobody could see who was giving what. Clara's arms burned. It was worse and better. Lydia pulled beside her, jaw set, and afterward, gasping, offered Clara her water bottle first, because Lydia always noticed who had gone longest without a drink.

Before the relay on Saturday, Clara stood on the block second in line, the warm-up lanes emptying below her, the crowd a low murmur under the ceiling lights. Reagan looked up at her from the water and said, "Ringelmann." Clara laughed, set her toes on the edge, and waited for the horn.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: For ideal parallel plates, the field also equals the charge per unit area on a plate divided by the permittivity of free space, about 8.85 × 10^-12 farads per metre.
story:
The problem on the bench sheet gave the charge on each plate, the area of each plate, and the distance between them, and asked for the field strength at the midpoint. Jordan read it twice, then turned the page over, looking for a voltage. There was none. He read it a third time.

"It's a mistake," Axel said, leaning across the aisle between their stations. "You can't get the field without the voltage. Every problem we've done all week was V over d." He snapped his calculator shut. "Tell Korhonen and he'll fix the sheet."

Mr. Korhonen was at the far end of the lab, supervising Britany at the electrostatics kit, and Jordan did get up to walk over there. Halfway across the room he stopped, because Britany was doing something with the electroscope and a silk cloth and it seemed a bad moment, and because a small, recalcitrant part of him resisted the idea of asking before he had even tried. He went back to his bench.

He wrote down what he had. Charge, Q. Area, A. Distance, d. He drew the plates in his notebook, two vertical lines, and marked the midpoint with an x. The field between charged plates pointed from the positive to the negative; that much he knew. The voltage was the energy per charge, and if he didn't have energy he couldn't use that route. But the charge itself was sitting there in front of him, doing something. It had to matter. A plate with more charge on it pushed harder. He divided Q by A in his notebook, almost without deciding to, and got a number that felt like a charge spread over a surface, a density of charge. Then he was stuck again.

The textbook was under a stack of handouts on the shelf behind him. He hadn't opened it since September, and the pages were marked with Britany's old pencil tabs from some previous year, which was pure happenstance, but the chapter on Gauss's law had a table of results in the margin. Parallel plates, it said, uniform field, E equals sigma over epsilon naught. The footnote spelled it out: for ideal parallel plates, the field also equals the charge per unit area on a plate divided by the permittivity of free space, about 8.85 × 10^-12 farads per metre. His sigma was Q over A, which he had already computed. He wrote the word permittivity carefully, the way he used to copy vocab in middle school.

"It's called the permittivity of free space," he said to Axel, holding up the book. "Eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve. Farads per metre." Axel squinted at the margin, then at Jordan's notebook, then pulled his own sheet toward him and started copying the numbers.

The division took Jordan eleven seconds. The field came out large, the way fields between close, highly charged plates did, and when he multiplied by d to see what voltage would have produced it, the answer was absurd, several hundred thousand volts. He checked the arithmetic twice. It was consistent. The plates in the problem were carrying a serious charge, and whoever wrote the sheet had simply never given them the number he'd been trained to reach for.

Mr. Korhonen came down the aisle and looked at Jordan's page without touching it. "Some of you found the charge route," he said. "Some found the voltage route. Both are on the sheet by design." He moved on to the next bench, and Jordan sat there with his answer circled, the number still on the display of his calculator. It was the same field either way, he supposed, the same push on a charge placed at the x between the plates, and yet the two ways of getting there felt different in his hands, one about energy, one about how much charge you could crowd onto a surface. He wasn't sure he could say which one was more true, or whether that question even meant anything. He copied the answer onto the sheet, and Britany, passing on her way to the sink, glanced at his page and said, "Same as mine."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In a standard repayment mortgage, early monthly payments go mostly toward interest, and later payments go mostly toward paying down the amount borrowed.
story:
Brooklyn stood in the doorway of Gillian's apartment holding a shoebox of flyers, because Gillian's mother had said someone should actually do something about the building, and Brooklyn had said she would, without knowing what doing something meant.

"Put them on the counter," Gillian said. "The landlord's coming at six."

The notice had gone up on Monday by the mailboxes: rent going up two hundred dollars in the fall. Gillian had photographed it and sent it to their group chat, and Arabella had replied with a single long line of exclamation points. Since then the three of them had been drafting a petition in the building's shared kitchen, which smelled of cabbage that seemed to ferment permanently in the corners, a smell Brooklyn had stopped noticing until she left and found it on her coat.

Arabella arrived with her laptop. "My cousin says we should all refuse to pay," she said. "A rent strike."

"She has a house," Gillian said. "She bought one last year."

"She says buying is why we're being stupid. Renting is throwing money away. Her exact words."

Brooklyn spread the flyers. At the top, in a font she'd argued with Arabella about, it said OUR HOMES ARE NOT GUARANTEED. Below that, the new rent, the old rent, and a line for signatures. She smoothed the paper flat with the heel of her hand.

"What does a house cost?" she asked. It came out more bluntly than she meant.

Arabella typed, then turned the screen. "Here. Condos in this neighborhood, seven hundred thousand, and you need a down payment first. Like ten percent. Seventy thousand dollars." She said the number and then laughed, a short sound with no humor in it, and shut the laptop halfway.

"Seventy thousand," Gillian repeated. She was leaning against the counter with her arms crossed, and Brooklyn noticed she was doing the math against something, her lips moving. Gillian's mother cleaned offices nights. "That's not saving up. That's a different life."

"But my cousin did it," Arabella said. "Her and Marcus. They had a deposit for the offer, a few thousand, and then the down payment, and the bank gave them the rest. A mortgage. Fifteen years of payments."

The landlord knocked at ten past six, early, holding a clipboard. Gillian's mother had not come home yet, which Brooklyn suspected was the point. He looked at the flyers on the counter and then at the three of them.

"You're the tenants' committee," he said. It wasn't a question.

"We're the tenants," Gillian said.

He explained the increase in the flat voice of a man reading from a script he hadn't written: costs, taxes, the market. Brooklyn watched his hands on the clipboard, and the word melancholic surfaced in her mind, which surprised her, because he didn't look sad. He looked tired in a way that had hardened into something else.

"My cousin pays fifteen hundred a month on her house," Arabella said, suddenly, to him. "That's more than our rent. So why is she allowed to complain less than us?"

"That's different," the landlord said. "That's her house."

Brooklyn had been quiet, and because she'd been quiet, everyone looked at her when she spoke. "My mom does our bookkeeping on the kitchen table," she said. "I looked at her mortgage statement once. Five years in." She stopped, unsure whether she was allowed to say the next part, and said it anyway. "Almost all of every payment had gone to interest. The amount she actually owed had barely moved. She paid all that time and she still owed nearly the whole thing."

The landlord shifted his weight.

"Then it flips," Brooklyn said. "Later the payments mostly go to paying down what she borrowed. The early years, the bank takes its share first." She had asked her mother about it once, and her mother had laughed, not kindly, and said welcome to being an adult. "So she's not really free either. It's just a longer rope."

"So renting is fine?" Arabella said. "That's your point?"

"No." Brooklyn looked at the flyers, at the line for signatures that was still empty. "My point is she can't leave and we can't stay, and everybody's paying somebody. That's all I've got."

The landlord said he'd pass the petition along, which all three of them knew meant nothing, and left. Through the window Brooklyn watched him cross the parking lot to a car that was nicer than any car parked in the lot.

Arabella opened the laptop again. "I'll print more flyers. My cousin can choke, by the way."

"She's not wrong that we need to own something eventually," Brooklyn said. "She's just wrong that it's simple."

Gillian took a pen and signed her own name on the first line, pressing hard enough that Brooklyn heard the nib catch on the paper.

"There," Gillian said. "Now it's started."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
Nathan had chosen the table by the window at the coffee shop because it was the only one with a plug, and because from there he could see the door. He had his laptop open to his email, inbox loaded, one message unread, and he had been looking at it for eleven minutes without clicking. Krystal came in with her scarf still zipped inside her jacket and dropped into the chair across from him, stealing his cup to smell it.

"You look phlegmatic," she said, handing it back. "Like a man at a bus stop."

"I'm fine."

"Fine means the email came." She said it the way she said everything, flat, as though she were only reading a sign aloud. Dale arrived a minute later with three hot chocolates he hadn't been asked for, sliding one in front of each of them like a lawyer presenting evidence. He sat down, saw the laptop, saw the unread count, and put both hands flat on the table.

"Open it."

"Not yet."

"You've been saying not yet since you got here," Krystal said. "The barista's watching you. She thinks you're going to cry into the machine."

He hadn't actually. The barista, a broad woman with gray in her braid, had glanced at him once. Nathan closed the laptop halfway, a turtle retreating, and Dale leaned back and groaned. Dale had applied to four schools, all within driving distance, all with rolling admission, all decided by October. He had the relaxed cruelty of someone whose future was already boring. "You're going to make us sit here while you decide whether to decide."

"Can you not verbalize every single thing you observe?" Nathan said, and Krystal laughed into her hot chocolate, and Dale grinned because being annoying was a kind of affection between them.

Ms. Doyle was two tables over with a paperback and a scone, and Nathan had noticed her without letting himself notice, the way you register a teacher outside school as something vaguely unreal, a painting that had wandered off its wall. She caught his eye and raised her mug a centimeter, a gesture so small it could be denied later.

Krystal pulled out her phone. "Okay, while you stall, tell me the thing from the tour again. The number thing."

"You want the number thing now."

"I'm doing your interview prep. If you get in, you get interviews, and you tell every story like it happened to someone else." She set the phone between them. "Go. Campus tour. The guide."

He let out a breath, and for a moment he was back there, October rain, the tour group huddled under an archway while the guide gestured at a quad. "So the guide's doing the whole pitch," he said. "She goes, and our incoming class, the quality, the selectivity, and then she says, and our yield this year, which is, you know, we're very proud. And this senior next to me, some guy visiting with his dad, just asks her, what's yield?" He turned his cup a quarter turn on its saucer. "And she gets this look, like she's been waiting all week for someone to ask. She says, yield is the percentage of students a college admits who then accept the offer and enroll."

Dale frowned. "That's it? That's the whole famous number?"

"That's the whole number," Nathan said. "The senior asks why she's proud of it, and she just does the smile again and moves on to the dining hall."

"It's a popularity contest," Krystal said, "measured in paperwork."

"It's more like an ego thing," Dale said. "The college wants to feel chosen. It's like," and he waved his hand around for the comparison, "like when you ask someone to prom and they say yes, and then you go around telling everyone the yes rate."

"You're an apologist," Krystal told him. "For institutions."

"I'm an apologist for people wanting to be liked. Colleges are people, kind of, legally."

It should have been funny, and it was, and Nathan laughed, but the laugh left a door open somewhere behind him, and through it came the thought he had been holding off all morning. The school had spent October telling a rain-soaked archway full of visitors how chosen it felt. If its yield mattered that much, then his unread email was not only an answer to him. He was also, right now, an answer to them, a fraction in somebody's spreadsheet, a yes or a no that would land in the numerator or the denominator. He was the chooser as much as the chosen, and nobody in the whole process had ever once put it that way, and it made him feel powerful and also slightly sick.

He opened the laptop.

The screen woke, the inbox still loaded, and Krystal reached across and put two fingers on his sleeve, not holding him, just touching, and Dale went quiet for the first time in recorded history, and the espresso machine behind the counter chose that moment to grind, a long roar that seemed to slow everything down. Nathan read the subject line. Then he read it again, because the first reading hadn't gone anywhere, it had just slid off. Krystal was saying his name. Ms. Doyle, he saw in the edge of his vision, had lowered her book.

"I got in," he said.

Krystal screamed, actually screamed, and the barista looked over, and Dale stood up and knocked his hot chocolate into Krystal's phone case, and neither of them cared. Ms. Doyle raised her mug another centimeter, which was her version of applause.

"And?" Krystal said, still gripping his sleeve. "You're going, right? You're going."

Nathan looked at the screen, at the word Congratulations doing its bright, confident work, and then he turned the laptop toward them so they could see it too, because he did not yet trust himself to be the only one holding it. "Can we just," he said. "Can we just sit here a minute. Before anybody says what it means."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The Haymarket affair in Chicago on May 4, 1886, grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday and is considered the origin of May 1 as International Workers' Day.
story:
The union hall smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, and Madison had been standing at the sign-in table for two hours before anyone told her what the vote was actually about. Her mother had said only, "Come after school, I need you to run the sheet," which meant checking names against the membership list, which meant standing near the door while three hundred people in warehouse uniforms filed past her into the hall.

"They're voting on whether to take the company's last offer," said Oskar, who had shown up with a clipboard he seemed to have appointed himself to. "Three percent, but they gut the overtime rules after eight hours. Anything past forty a week goes to straight time." He said it the way he said everything in econ class, like he was reading from an invisible textbook, and Madison hated and relied on it in equal measure.

"Which is the exact thing the whole contract exists to prevent," said Abhijot, folding a flyer into eighths. "Collective bargaining means the union negotiates for everybody at once, so the company can't just pick off whoever's desperate. If the vote fails, they go back to the table. If it fails badly, they might strike." She said "strike" quietly, the way people say a word they've only just started believing could apply to them.

Madison stamped another name. Her mother was somewhere near the front, in the row of shop stewards, and had not looked back once. What Madison kept returning to was Saturday, when she'd watched footage of workers marching in Jakarta and Berlin and São Paulo, all on the same day, and asked her mother why so many countries picked May 1, and her mother had said, "Look it up, Maddie, I'm ironing." Which had felt, at the time, like a small cruelty, and now felt like something else.

Ms. Xu, who taught down the hall from Ms. Nobody and lived two doors from the hall itself, came through the line with her retirement fund badge clipped sideways. "Do you know the answer yet?" she asked Madison, because Ms. Xu was the sort of adult who remembered questions you'd asked in October.

"The marching thing? I found it. Chicago, 1886." Madison kept her voice low. "There was this affair at Haymarket, May 4th. It grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday. That's where May 1 as International Workers' Day comes from. People in other countries got a holiday out of it and we got, like, a mattress sale."

Abhijot tilted her head. "So the eight-hour day, the thing your mom's whole contract is defending, started with people getting killed at a protest."

"It problematizes the three percent, that's for sure," Oskar said, and for once Madison thought he'd earned the word. He wasn't using it to sound smart; he meant that knowing where the eight-hour day came from made the company's offer harder to look at as just a number.

A man in a hi-vis vest near the mic said the eight-hour day was spoiled entitlement anyway, that his grandfather worked sunup to sundown and was happy, and Oskar leaned over and murmured, "Nostalgia for backbreaking labor is just hedonism for people who like suffering in the past tense," which made Abhijot snort and made Madison write it on the back of the membership sheet, next to a doodle of a fist.

The debate ran long. Someone argued that genetics made some people suited to night shifts, actually, taller heartier stock, and Abhijot, who wanted to do genetics, said "phenotypic variation doesn't schedule your shifts, the contract does," and got a small round of applause, and the mic moved on. What Madison noticed, standing at the door, was that the hall was not one crowd. There were the older workers who talked about 1994 like scripture, the new hires who checked their phones, the stewards like her mother who did arithmetic on legal pads. They wanted different things. She understood that the vote would force them to want one thing together, or reveal that they couldn't.

The tally took eleven minutes. Madison counted the raised hands herself, because nobody had told her to and because she could not stand not knowing. When the teller announced that the offer had failed by nineteen votes, the hall made a sound she had never heard before, half cheer and half intake of breath, and her mother turned around at last, found her by the door, and did not smile or frown, only nodded, once, like someone confirming a measurement.

Outside, in the parking lot, Oskar asked what happens next. Madison watched her mother and the other stewards walk back inside with the legal pads.

"Either they bargain again or we don't shop here for a while," she said. "Hand me the clipboard."

"May 1st," Abhijot said, zipping her jacket. "We should march. All of us. This year."

Madison looked at the lit door of the hall, then at the dark street.

"Get the dates right," she said. "May 4th was Haymarket. The day they marched for was May 1st."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Sorting a list takes more work than one linear search, so sorting just to run binary search pays off only when the same data will be searched many times.
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm plastic and the janitor's lemon spray, and Payton had eleven minutes to decide whether to sort. The regional programming competition started at four, and the practice problem on her screen held a list of forty thousand patient records, unsorted, and a single query: find record 38102. Khushi leaned across the aisle with the confidence of someone who had watched a video about binary search the night before.

"Sort it first," Khushi said. "Then binary search. Cut the list in half, then in half again. It's elegant."

"Elegant," Madeleine repeated from the next row, not looking up. "Grandiose is what it is. You want to rebuild the whole list to answer one question."

Payton put her hands flat on the keyboard, which was a habit she had picked up from her mother, a physical therapist who claimed the physiology of the wrists obeyed the same rules in surgeons and in teenagers who typed too fast. In her first year of high school Payton had inured herself to losing these arguments by always deferring to whoever spoke loudest, and she could feel that old reflex starting up now, her mouth already shaping the word "okay." She stopped it.

"Run both," she said instead. "Madeleine, do the linear search. Khushi, sort and then binary search. Same list, same target."

Madeleine finished first by a wide margin. On the screen her program walked the list item by item and found the record in a fraction of a second, while Khushi's code was still in the middle of its sort. Khushi's program eventually finished too, and its actual search, when it came, was startlingly quick, a knife going through butter. But the total time belonged to Madeleine, and they all sat with that for a moment.

"So binary search is slower," Khushi said, in the tone of someone whose video had betrayed her.

"No," Payton said slowly. "The search is faster. The sorting is the slow part." She was building the sentence as she spoke it, the way she built code, testing each piece. "Sorting the list takes more work than one linear search. So if you're searching once, sorting just to run binary search, you lose. It only pays off when you'll search the same data many times."

The room went quiet in the particular way it did when Ms. Somsak walked the rows, hands clasped behind her, reading screens without comment. She paused at Payton's monitor, looked for three seconds at the two timings displayed side by side, and moved on. Payton felt absurdly pleased, then annoyed at herself for feeling pleased, then pleased again anyway.

"The real problem," Madeleine said, spinning her chair, "asks for six hundred queries on the same list."

They all looked at the actual competition problem, the one behind the practice one, the one due in ninety minutes. Six hundred queries. Payton pulled up a fresh file and started writing the sort before anyone had agreed to anything, and Khushi laughed, and Madeleine said, "I take it back, the grand plan lives." Somewhere behind them Ms. Somsak said, "Eleven minutes to deadline, ladies," though there were ninety, and everyone knew there were ninety, and no one corrected her.

Payton typed the binary search with her wrists flat and her mind moving between the two timings on the screen, the walk and the knife, wondering which one she would have trusted yesterday. "Copy the list to my machine," she said. "We're searching it six hundred times."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Heating and cooling bills change with the seasons, so averaging a full year of bills gives a truer monthly cost than a single month's bill.
story:
Carson sat in the orange plastic chair by the window of Highway One Driving School, waiting for his four o'clock lesson, with two apartment leases fanned out on his knee. His mother had handed them to him that morning at breakfast with the particular look she reserved for requests she felt guilty making. The landlord wanted an answer by five, and she was at work until six, so the decision had landed on him the way things landed on him lately, without ceremony and with a deadline. He spread the pages across the seat beside him. The first apartment, on Delmore Street, was nine hundred a month plus utilities. The second, on Fenwick, was nine sixty with water included but heat and electricity separate.

He had started a table in the back of his notebook, the same notebook where he was supposed to be reviewing the chapter on right-of-way at four-way stops. Then his phone buzzed. It was Leah, who had moved into her own place in June and had become, in the months since, voluble on the subject of adult life, narrating grocery prices and bus schedules to anyone who would hold still. "Did you figure out which one is cheaper," she wrote. "Fenwick looks better on paper but paper lies."

He typed back that the paper was all he had. The Delmore lease included a printout of bills from the current tenant, and he'd been staring at the July line when his grandfather, who had insisted on being kept informed of the whole affair, texted him a message that read like a letter, because his grandfather had never learned to write anything short. "I saw the summer gas bill you sent me," it said. "Twelve dollars and some change. Don't you trust that number, boy. Your grandmother and I had a July bill like that once and we about fainted in January when the real one came. Ask for all twelve months, add every one, and divide by twelve. Heating and cooling change with the seasons, so one month of bills tells you almost nothing. A full year, averaged, that's the only honest monthly number there is."

Carson read it twice. He looked at the July figure again, then flipped the printout over, and there on the back, faintly photocopied, was a second page he had missed at the breakfast table: the whole year of bills, month stacked on month. He copied them down in his notebook, all twelve, and added them in the margin of his right-of-way chapter, under a diagram of a stop sign. Some were small, some were three and four times the small ones, and when he divided the total by twelve, the honest monthly cost for Delmore came out higher than the July bill alone would ever have suggested. He did the same arithmetic for Fenwick, where the leasing office had given his mother only one sample bill, from August, and he understood suddenly that he could not make the two apartments speak the same language. One was telling him the truth across a year. The other was telling him one flattering month.

Eshal texted a photo of the parking lot outside his own driving school across town, with the caption "wish me luck, parallel parking," and Carson almost envied him the simplicity of cones and painted lines. He wrote back: "Which is cheaper, an apartment that tells you the whole year or one that shows you a single month?" Eshal replied with a row of question marks, then, a minute later, "the year one, obviously, but is the year one also the more expensive apartment? Because that's the real question." That was Eshal, who could destabilize a settled thing with one sentence. Carson had been treating cheaper as the answer, and now he stood in the question again: the Delmore with its averaged, honest, higher number, or the Fenwick, whose real cost he could only estimate, whose August bill sat on his page like a smile with the rest of the face cropped out.

The door to the driving school opened and Ms. Lindqvist leaned out, keys in hand, and said, "Carson, you're up, car three." He gathered the leases, folded the notebook around them, and followed her out to the lot, still doing sums in his head. Behind the wheel, checking mirrors in the order she demanded, he found his attention splitting, one half on the wheel and one half on twelve numbers arranged like a strange skyline, low in summer, tall in winter. When she asked him to pull out, he did it cleanly, and she made a small sound of approval. "You're quieter than usual," she said. "Half here, half somewhere else."

"Deciding between two apartments," he said, and signaled, and checked the blind spot. "My mom has to sign by five."

"Two leases," she said. "The one with the full year of bills in front of you, or the one without?"

He laughed, surprised. "How did you know that's the choice?"

"Because it's always the choice," she said, and pointed at the intersection ahead. "Left here, and check your mirror before you brake."

He took the left. He had ten minutes of driving left and an hour before five, and he had decided nothing except this: that the low summer bill was a kind of attrition he hadn't known to guard against, one month wearing away the truth of eleven others. At the next red light he pulled out his phone, held it low, and texted his mother: "Delmore. Ask Fenwick for all twelve months of bills before you rule it out, but go with the one that already told us everything." The light turned green, and Ms. Lindqvist said, "Phone away, eyes up," and he pulled forward into the intersection, both hands on the wheel, the message gone.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
story:
The parish hall smelled of coffee and funeral casseroles, and Michael stood by the folding table with his tie loosened, holding a paper cup he had no intention of drinking from. His grandmother's coffin was already out in the sanctuary, closed now, the flowers being carried to the altar by women in their seventies who had known her since before he was born. Leland had come because Michael had asked him to, and Leland was telling a story about the time a substitute teacher had mistyped his own name on the attendance sheet, and Michael had laughed. Out loud. In the middle of the receiving line, three rows from where his father was shaking hands and saying thank you, thank you.

He set the cup down on the tablecloth and felt the laugh still in his chest like something stolen. His grandmother had been dead for nine days. He had watched her decline through the last spring, had sat beside her hospital bed while she told, in a voice worn thin, the same stories she always told, and now he was laughing at a typo in a church basement while her photograph stood on an easel near the door. The photograph was from her sixtieth birthday, when she had still been the family's great raconteur, the one who could hold a whole Christmas dinner hostage for forty minutes with the tale of the runaway turkey, and everyone glad to be held.

"You okay?" Leland asked, quiet enough that only Michael could hear it.

"Yeah. No. I don't know." He looked toward the easel. "It's been a week and a half. She's not even cold yet, and I'm over here cracking up."

Camelia appeared beside them with two oatmeal cookies and gave one to each of them without asking, which was how she did most things. She had come to the funeral even though she had only met his grandmother once, at a school concert, when his grandmother had told her she had good posture and meant it as a compliment. "My aunt was in here earlier," Camelia said. "She's a grief counselor. She left some of her pamphlets on that table by the coat rack, and I read one while I was hiding from your cousin, the belligerent one who kept arguing about the parking."

"The parking was bad," Leland said.

"The parking was fine." Camelia brushed crumbs off her fingers. "Anyway. The pamphlet was about this thing Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut wrote, the dual process model. It says grieving people move back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, instead of moving in one direction. Like a pendulum, kind of. Not down a staircase."

Michael turned the paper cup a quarter turn on the table. "So it's not a betrayal," he said. "The laughing."

"I mean, I'm not a counselor. But the pamphlet didn't seem to think anybody needed to be fixed. It was actually kind of anti that. It didn't pathologize people for going back to normal for an afternoon." She shrugged. "My aunt got mad at a different book once for making grief sound like a syllabus."

He left them by the coffee and walked through the swinging door into the sanctuary, where the flowers were being arranged and a few people knelt in the pews. The coffin was at the front, and he went up the aisle slowly, letting his shoes be loud on the stone, because his grandmother had always said a boy should announce himself. He had not cried yet. He had expected to cry at the hospital, at the funeral home, at the burial, and each time the tears had not come, and he had wondered whether something in him was broken, whether the version of himself who loved her was somehow less than he had believed. Now he stood at the head of the coffin and put his hand flat on the wood, which was cold, which was polished, which was nothing like her hand.

He thought about laughing again. He thought about the pendulum, if that was what it was, swinging between this moment and the moment with Leland by the coffee, and he understood that neither one was false. He could stand here facing her, and he could go back out there and be sixteen and hungry and amused by a typo, and the swinging itself was the grief, not a detour around it. What he could not decide, what stayed unresolved even as the organist began to play softly somewhere behind him, was whether that made it bearable or merely ongoing, whether his grandmother, who had buried a husband and two brothers and never once described it to him, had known this all along and said nothing.

"She would have liked that you laughed," said his father, who had come up the aisle behind him without announcing himself at all. "She hated a room where nobody did."

Michael took his hand off the coffin and looked at the flowers, the white ones she had grown from seed every year along the back fence. "Dad, do you want to get food after this? Real food. Not casserole."

His father put an arm around his shoulders. "She'd want us to order the extra garlic bread in her honor."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills.
story:
Madison had twelve minutes to find her grandfather's discharge papers before the graduation line formed, and the trophy case in the main hallway was reflecting her panic back at her in triplicate.

"He keeps them in the cedar box, right?" George asked, holding her cap while she crouched at the pay phone alcove, calling the house for the third time. Her grandmother picked up, breathless, and said her grandfather was already on his way, that he'd left twenty minutes ago with the box under his arm like a church casserole, and that Madison should stop calling and go stand in line.

The problem was the speech. She had written it in April, when the assignment from Ms. Charles had seemed abstract: say something true about what a diploma means. She had written about endurance, about four years of attendance codes and standardized rubrics, and she had been proud of its clean, confident cadences. Then last night at dinner, her grandfather had mentioned, almost in passing, that he never got a diploma at all, that after the war he earned a GED, and Madison had felt her whole speech go hollow in her hands. She'd looked it up at midnight: the GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills. He had been seventeen when he enlisted, eighteen when the tests were new, and he had come home and proven himself to a piece of paper years before Madison was born.

"Move it, graduates," the vice principal called, herding them toward the gym. Noelle grabbed Madison's sleeve. "You're fourth. If you're going to rewrite the thing, you have about nine minutes."

The hallway smelled like floor wax and carnations. Madison sat on the bench beneath the framed photos of graduating classes going back decades, all those vestigial evidence of ceremony, and pulled out her phone. The original draft glowed there, polished and dead. She could say the tidy version, the one everyone expected, the one Ms. Charles had praised as "assured." Or she could say something about her grandfather, though she wasn't sure she could do it without sentimentality, without turning him into a prop. She had once argued in an essay that schools had a habit of pathologizing every departure from the standard route, and now she was sitting in a hallway built entirely around the standard route, wearing a rented robe, and she didn't know if her own argument was insight or just a girl wanting her grandfather in her speech.

He appeared at the far end of the corridor, moving slowly with his cane, the cedar box actually under his arm. "You didn't have to bring it," she said, standing, but he was already pressing the discharge papers and the old certificate into her hands. "You said on the phone you wanted to check the date," he said. "1953. I took the tests late. It's not a war story, Maddie. It's just what I did."

"Mr. Alvarez's class is going in," Noelle said, hovering. "Two minutes."

Madison looked down at the certificate, the creases like river deltas across it. "What was it like," she asked, "walking into a room and just proving it, no four years?"

He shrugged. "Faster. Lonelier. Both." He straightened her cap, which George had jammed on sideways. "Say whatever you want up there. The paper isn't the point. It never was."

That wasn't quite true, and she knew it, and she loved him for saying it anyway. The paper mattered; she had worked for it, and the tests he took mattered too, because without them the country would have had nothing to offer him but gratitude, which does not get you a job. She folded the new speech in her mind as they walked toward the gym doors: not a rejection of the first draft, but the two of them overlapping, her grandfather's hallway and hers, the same threshold.

Inside, the seats were filling. The vice principal was saying something about seating order, and Madison realized with a lurch that she was supposed to be in line already, that Noelle had gone ahead, that George was holding the doors. "Fourth," she mouthed to the woman at the program table, and the woman pointed, and Madison started down the center aisle, certificate still in her hand because there was nowhere to put it.

Her grandfather took a seat at the back, leaning the cane against the bleachers. From the stage, later, she would hold the microphone and begin the old speech, then pause, then set the folded pages face-down on the podium and lift the certificate instead, saying, "This belongs to a graduate too." But right now she was still walking, the paper crinkling with every step, and the aisle was long, and the first notes of the processional were starting up behind her.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: False friends are words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning; Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, not embarrassed.
story:
The Spanish room smelled of dust and radiator heat, and Oliver had claimed the far carrel in the school library three weeks ago, when the debate assignment was still an abstraction rather than a clock ticking in his chest. Five minutes, entirely in Spanish, on municipal water privatization. He had chosen the topic because Mr. Farah said it was current, and because the Spanish vocabulary for water, contracts, and public trust had begun to feel like a second skin, thin but wearable.

His opening argument survived the first rehearsal. By the second, it collapsed, and Haley, who was marking his pauses in pencil from across the table, looked up at the sound of his pen stopping. "You lost the thread," she said, not unkindly. She slid her water bottle toward him, because she had noticed he never remembered to bring one, and because his voice thinned when he went too long without drinking.

"La empresa es embarazada," he began again, meaning to say the company was compromised, or perhaps embarrassed by its own records, and Haley set down her pencil. Around them, two students from the study group Dimitrios had assembled turned in their chairs, and one of them laughed, quickly covering her mouth.

"What," Oliver said. "What did I say."

Dimitrios arrived late, coat still buttoned, holding the handout from their Spanish seminar. "False friends," he said, tapping the page. "Words that look alike in two languages but mean different things. Embarazada means pregnant, not embarrassed." He said it the way he said everything, flat and certain, and Oliver stared at the word in the margin, embarazada, so reasonable, so obviously cognate with embarrassed, and felt the ground under his argument shift.

He spent the next twenty minutes rebuilding the sentence. The company was not pregnant; the company had misled the city, and he searched his notes for the verb he actually meant. In the process he reread the whole case for privatization, the one he was arguing against, because Haley had suggested that a debater who could not state the opposing view fairly was merely reciting. She had used the word "reciting" with a small grimace, and he had not liked it, and had known she was right. The pro-privatization side was not a cartoon of greed. It was parsimonious, in its way: one contract, one provider, lower overhead, faster repairs. He would have to impugn it without pretending it was stupid, which was harder than calling it evil.

Mr. Farah drifted past the carrels on his rounds, pausing at their table long enough to hear Oliver run the middle section twice. "Slower," was all he said, and then, nodding at Haley's marked-up transcript, "Keep that." He moved on to shelve a returned atlas, and Oliver understood that the pace mattered more than the vocabulary now, that five minutes of steady Spanish would beat six minutes of brilliant Spanish delivered at a sprint.

On the day itself, the library's small presentation room held nine students and Mr. Farah by the window. Oliver stood, and the sunlight through the blinds striped the table, and he began. He gave the opposing view its due, cleanly, in his rebuilt sentences, and then he took it apart, and his hands stopped shaking around the second minute. In the fourth minute, arguing that the city's own repair records had been adequate, he said the word "embarazada" once, deliberately, paused, and nine students held their breath, and he said, "Quiero decir," and corrected himself, and the laughter that came was with him, warm, the laugh of people who had all made some version of the same mistake.

He finished with eleven seconds left on the clock, and Haley caught his eye from the second row and raised her pencil, which was her way of applauding. Mr. Farah made a note on his clipboard and did not say what it was.

Afterward, in the emptying room, Dimitrios gathered the handouts and stopped at the last page. "You know," he said, "for the final exam, they've switched the topic." He handed Oliver the sheet. "Marriage customs across cultures. Five minutes, in Spanish." Oliver looked at the topic, looked at his notes still open to embarazada, and began, very quietly, to laugh.

"Somebody in that exam room," he said, "is going to tell the whole class the bride was embarrassed."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
story:
Elliot had spent three weeks building a Plexiglas box with two chambers, a hot plate, a thermometer, and a rack of cobalt chloride tubes, and by eleven a.m. on science fair day the box still looked, in his own private opinion, like a fish tank that had given up on fish. He set it on table fourteen and tried to burnish the scratched lid with the sleeve of his good shirt, which only smeared the scratches into a soft haze.

"You're polishing Plexiglas with cotton," said Zac, arriving with a duffel bag and a box of borrowed hot mitts. "That's like washing a car with a brick."

"It's called presentation," Elliot said. "Mr. Park marks presentation."

The demonstration was simple, which had been the whole argument. The solution in the tubes was pink at room temperature, and the reaction that made the blue form was endothermic, meaning it drank heat. The question, the one printed on his display board under the heading WHICH WAY?, was what would happen when he warmed it. Zac insisted the heat would push the reaction backward, because heat was "like pressure, it shoves everything away." Ryan, who had read the textbook chapter twice out of spite, said no: if the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products. Elliot had written both predictions on the board, side by side, and left a blank line under RESULTS, which he now regretted, because a blank line in marker is a very public thing.

They were arguing about it when Ryan showed up with a note folded into a triangle, tossed it across the table, and walked off toward the bake sale without a word. Elliot unfolded it. "Zac is wrong but he is my cousin's friend so be nice. Also I looked it up again at 2 a.m. If forward is endothermic, heating it shifts it toward products. Blue. Don't tell him I told you. Burn this." He did not burn it. He folded it into his pocket, where it sat against his hip like a small warm verdict.

The gym filled up. Parents drifted past with coffee. A girl from the robotics club dropped a gear on the floor and it rolled, improbably, all the way to table fourteen and stopped against the leg, as if it too wanted to know about temperature. Mr. Park arrived at twelve fifteen with a clipboard and the unhurried air of a judge who has seen four hundred volcanoes in his life and is braced for the four hundred and first.

"So," Mr. Park said. "Le Chatelier. Tell me what you expect."

Before Elliot could answer, Zac leaned in. "He thinks it goes blue. I say it goes more pink. Heat pushes it back. That's just thermodynamics, sir. Basic chemical jurisprudence."

"It is not jurisprudence," Ryan called from across the aisle, betraying his position and his 2 a.m. research in one breath.

Elliot laughed, and found that laughing steadied him. "Here's the thing," he said, and he meant it, which surprised him. "Zac thinks about it like shoving. Ryan thinks about it like the reaction wanting something, like heat is a thing it can eat. I've been going back and forth all week, and honestly I can hold both in my head at once, which is a horrible place to be. So." He snapped on the impermeable gloves his mother had insisted on, lifted the first tube with the tongs, and lowered it into the warm chamber.

For three seconds nothing happened, and Elliot experienced those three seconds as a kind of personal drought. Then the pink began to go lavender at the bottom of the tube, then violet, then a clean startling blue, climbing the liquid like dusk climbing a window. Zac made a low noise, half groan, half respect. Mr. Park wrote something on his clipboard and did not smile, but his pen moved in a way that seemed friendly.

"It goes toward the products," Ryan shouted from across the aisle. "Blue side. I said blue!"

"You said blue at two in the morning, next to your note," Elliot said, and pulled the folded triangle from his pocket and held it up, and the whole aisle saw the words BURN THIS in Ryan's handwriting, and Ryan came over the tables rather than around them to try to snatch it, and Zac was laughing so hard he had to sit on the edge of the fish tank that had given up on fish, and Mr. Park said, "Careful, that's somebody's equilibrium you're sitting on," and reached for the second tube himself.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, the US unemployment rate was 3.9 percent for workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma and 5.6 percent for those without one.
story:
Nicole sat on the trunk of her mother's car with her gown bunched around her knees, the mortarboard already sliding off her head, and watched Mahmoud lean against the light pole at the edge of the senior lot. He had texted her that morning, just the word congratulations and a question mark, as if he were checking whether he was still allowed to say it. He had left school in November of junior year, and since then his appearances had the quality of a rumor: brief, secondhand, hard to verify.

She had her own reasons to stay put on the hot metal. Her mother was inside the gymnasium saving seats, and Nicole had promised Reagan she would wait here, and waiting was easier than joining the line of girls photographing each other's sashes in the shade of the oak. She had, in fact, spent the last week being photographed against her will, and she was beginning to feel like a monument to somebody else's satisfaction.

"You look like a judge," Mahmoud said, crossing the lot. He had a paper cup of gas station coffee and a sunburn.

"I look like a baked potato." She scooted over to make room on the trunk, and he sat, careful with his coffee, leaving a courteous gap between them that neither of them acknowledged.

He asked how the speeches had been, and she told him the vice principal had mispronounced six names and called a student named Gonzalez "Gonzaleez," twice, with confidence. He laughed, then went quiet in a way she recognized, and she let the quiet sit, because she had known him since eighth grade and knew that his real subject would arrive on its own schedule. It did. He said job hunting had been brutal. He'd applied to forty-one places since January. The warehouse wanted experience. The auto shop wanted certification. He said he'd read something that disabused him of the idea that the market was just hard for everyone, equally, the way people liked to say at the bus stop. He'd found a statistic. "For workers twenty-five and up, unemployment was 3.9 percent last year for people with a high school diploma. Without one, 5.6 percent." He turned the cup in his hands. "A guy at the staffing office had it taped to his monitor."

"So one point seven," Nicole said, before she'd fully decided to say anything.

"One point seven," he agreed. "Which sounds tiny until you're inside it." He didn't say it bitterly, which somehow made it worse. He said it the way you report weather.

Reagan arrived then, cap sideways, holding her phone up before she'd finished saying Nicole's name, and made them both squint through a photo Nicole would never ask to see. Reagan was going to the state school in the fall, and Mahmoud congratulated her with such completeness that Reagan's cheer faltered for a second, and Nicole watched her recover, watchfully, the way people do when they're trying not to be careful.

Ms. Quinn came through the lot collecting traffic cones in her cap and gown, an image Nicole filed away as the most honest thing she'd seen all day. Ms. Quinn stopped, said she was glad to see Mahmoud, said it plainly, without the softness people usually ladled over him, and told him the community college enrollment window was open until August if he ever wanted to finish, and that she'd waive the counselor appointment herself. It wasn't a speech. It was closer to an injunction, delivered at cone-collecting speed, and then she was gone toward the gymnasium with four cones stacked on her arm like trophies.

Nicole had spent the year treating graduation as an exit, a door she was being pushed through, and she had privately considered herself disaffected, above the ceremony of it, the way she considered herself above pep rallies and yearbook signing day. But the numbers Mahmoud had carried across the lot did something to the day. Not guilt, exactly. Her diploma and his absence were not the same fact, and she refused to pretend they were, refused to make her sitting here in polyester a moral achievement. And yet the lot had two kinds of people in it this morning, and she was on the trunk of a car in a gown, and he was leaning on a pole with gas station coffee, and the difference between them had been measured, publicly, to a decimal. She held both thoughts without forcing them into one comfortable shape, and found she could do that, and it didn't resolve anything, and the day went on anyway.

"One point seven," she said to Mahmoud, when Reagan had drifted off toward the oak.

"One point seven," he said, and lifted his cup toward her mortarboard, a small toast. "Nice baked potato."

"You should come to the thing at Reagan's," Nicole said. "There's supposed to be a taco guy."

Mahmoud looked at the light pole, then at the gymnasium doors where the music had started, and shook the last of his coffee around the bottom of the cup.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent.
story:
Blake had been sitting at the bus stop for eleven minutes when Simeon dropped onto the bench beside him, car keys spinning around one finger. The morning was warm enough that the fog over the soccer field had gone diaphanous, thinning to a gauze the sun could get through, and the Route 12 was, as always, late.

"You want the good news or the bad news," Simeon said. "The good news is my mom's letting me take her car Thursday. The bad news is it's Thursday morning, which means we miss first period."

"That's more good news."

"See, that's the attitude of a guy who hasn't failed his test twice." Simeon let the keys settle in his palm. "Daisy says you kept stalling at the merge."

"I didn't stall. I stopped." Blake watched a jogger cross at the far light, arms pumping like the crossing light had personally insulted her. "The on-ramp was short and there was a semi and I just stopped. The examiner wrote something down for a long time. That's never good, when they write for a long time."

His father's theory was that Blake thought too much, that driving was instinct and instinct came from the body, not from a mind running commentary on itself. His mother's theory was that he needed more practice, more repetitions, more miles. Blake privately suspected both were ways of not saying the simpler thing, which was that he was afraid of the car, though afraid wasn't quite it either. He was afraid of the other cars, all the strangers whose fenders he could bend.

They took the 12 to the lot behind the community college, where Simeon's mother's sedan sat waiting because she'd left it there and taken the light rail in. Parallel parking first. Simeon stood at the curb with a recycling bin he'd carried from the shelter of the bus stop, placing it where the rear tire of an imaginary parked car would be, and Blake practiced backing around it, adjusting the mirror so he could see the bin's edge, straightening, starting over.

"You're getting closer every time," Simeon said, which was true in both senses, the encouraging one and the literal one. On the sixth attempt Blake cleared the bin by four inches and sat there with the wheel centered, engine idling, something loosening in his shoulders.

Then the highway. Simeon directed him onto the ramp for the interstate, and almost immediately the traffic thickened and slowed, because a lane was closed ahead for repaving, cones marching along the right side like something out of antiquity, a ruin that had been there forever and would be there forever. A sign ordered MERGE LEFT. Most drivers obeyed it early, sliding over at the first gap, and the left lane lengthened into a long, patient caterpillar while the right lane sat nearly empty, shining and unused.

Blake signaled and began to drift toward the left, and then stopped himself, because a thought arrived that felt almost physical. All those cars in the right lane, all that empty road. He had read something, half-remembered, from a night of scrolling instead of sleeping. He took out his phone at a standstill and read it aloud, careful to get it right. "Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent."

"Zipper merge," Simeon repeated, as though tasting the words. "So the sign's basically a lie."

"The sign's the polite version." Blake put the phone down. "The zipper merge is the real version." He signaled off. Rolled forward in the empty lane, past cars whose drivers would not look at him, one man laying on his horn as though Blake had stolen something from him personally, though all Blake had stolen was forty percent of the road the man wasn't using. At the cones, where the lanes finally pinched shut, a woman in a hatchback left him a gap, one car's length, and took her turn after him, and it did feel like a zipper, teeth interlocking, and the whole slow mass of them moved instead of standing.

He tried to understand why the horn still bothered him. His father would have said the man was valorizing the rules, treating early merging as a virtue and anyone who waited as a cheat, and maybe that was fair, or maybe the man just felt wronged and didn't care about departments of transportation. Blake couldn't decide, and he noticed that he couldn't decide, and let that be what it was. The fact of the 40 percent stood on one side of the scale and the man's fury stood on the other, and they didn't measure against each other in any unit he had.

They came back through town and Blake parallel parked the sedan at the curb by the bus stop, one clean motion, the recycling bin now replaced by an actual parked truck, four inches from its fender. He shut off the engine and sat with his hands still on the wheel.

"Thursday," Simeon said. "First period. You, me, the interstate."

"Both lanes," Blake said. "All the way to the merge point."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: US employers must generally give each employee a Form W-2 by the end of January, showing the previous year's wages and the taxes withheld, which is needed to file a tax return.
story:
The pharmacy's stockroom was subterranean, a windowless basement where Leah spent her Saturday mornings hauling boxes of shampoo up a metal staircase two at a time. She had taken the job in June because Ms. Do paid a dollar above minimum wage and because the register receipts fascinated her in a way she didn't admit to anyone. Every slip of paper itemized the shampoo, the cold medicine, the candy bars, and then added a line for sales tax, a small percentage that quietly raised the total. Nobody ever complained about it. People just paid, took their bags, and left.

Layla, who ran the front register, had a theory about that. "They don't see it as money," she said one afternoon during a lull, tearing the tape off a finished roll. "They see it as weather. Something that just happens to the price." Layla was saving for a used car and tracked every dollar of her own, but she had a soft spot for customers who came up short at the register, which was exactly why Ms. Do had quietly moved her off the express lane twice.

Leah's own money had a destination: the deposit for a summer field course on the coast, due in March. She had almost enough, and then she didn't, because her mother's car needed a brake job in February. What Leah remembered, dimly, was that some of the money she'd earned had been taken out of her paycheques all along. She dug the stubs out of her backpack and spread them across her bed. Gross pay, and then a column of deductions, federal income tax withheld among them, like the sales tax line on a receipt but running the other direction, money subtracted instead of added. She had a memory of her mother saying you could get some of it back, if you filed. Filed what, Leah didn't know.

"Ask Ms. Do," Layla said when Leah mentioned it, restocking the gum wall without looking up. "She handles all that."

Ms. Do was in her office above the dispensary, a narrow room with a calendar of national parks and a fan that rattled. "You mean your W-2," she said. "Employers have to give each employee one by the end of January. It shows your wages for the previous year and the taxes that were withheld. You need it to file your return."

"January," Leah repeated. It was the second week of February.

"It was mailed to the address we had on file."

Leah's stomach dropped. She had moved in November, from her mother's apartment to her aunt's place across town, and had updated her emergency contact but apparently nothing else. "I never got it."

Ms. Do pulled up a screen, typed, frowned. "It went to the old address." She was already reaching for her jacket. "Come back Thursday. I'll have a copy printed."

Thursday stretched out ahead of her like a held breath. On Wednesday Kristopher, who worked the evening shift and was angling for Leah's Saturday hours, cornered her by the basement stairs. "You're leaving, right? For the coast thing? So you don't need Saturdays anymore."

"I haven't left yet."

"But when you do." He leaned against the shelving. "Just tell her I asked first. Before Layla asks. Layla always asks."

Leah had seen how Kristopher's shifts got cut in January, how he'd started riding his bike eleven miles because the bus fare added up. She also knew Layla was saving for the car. She said, "Nobody's asked me anything," and carried her box up the stairs, though she hated herself a little for the dodge, and hated a little more that she'd noticed it, the small way people stigmatized whoever said no, as if choosing your own survival made you the difficult one.

Thursday, Ms. Do handed her a single sheet, warm from the printer. "Your wages and your withholding," she said. "Take it to whoever does the return." Leah's mother had said something about the free help session at the library downtown, two blocks from the magistrate's office where she worked as a clerk and where, she liked to joke, people argued about money all day with straight faces.

Leah filed that Saturday morning before her shift, in the library's carpeted basement, a different subterranean room, one with skylights punched through the ceiling that made coins of light on the floor. A volunteer walked her through the form, line by line. When she finished, the woman at the desk looked at the screen and said, "You're getting a refund."

"How much?"

The woman told her. It was not the whole deposit, but it was most of it, and the remainder was in Leah's savings account, and the course had a spot with her name on it if she paid by the fifteenth. She walked the two blocks to the courthouse and found her mother in the clerk's office, slid the refund confirmation across the counter between a stapler and a tray of pens.

Her mother read it, then read it again. "You did this yourself?"

"Mostly."

Her mother signed out at the desk, took her jacket off the hook, and said, "Come on. We're going to the bank before it closes."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
Colton had spread the two articles across the kitchen table like opposing counsel, which was a generous metaphor for what they actually were: a red folder containing a 2016 paper arguing that later school start times improved adolescent sleep, and a blue folder containing a 2019 paper, on essentially the same question, that found almost nothing. His mother kept walking through to get to the laundry room, and each time she paused at the angle of his elbows, as though the posture itself were the assignment.

"Due Monday?" she asked.

"Due Monday," he said, and she nodded the way people nod at weather they can't control.

The assignment from Mr. Bighorn was to write a critical review comparing the two, and Colton had assumed the hard part would be the prose. It was not the prose. The hard part was that both papers looked competent. Both had methods sections, both had statistics he could half-follow, both cited overlapping sources, and yet one said the effect was real and sizeable while the other said the evidence was thin. He had been taught his whole life that the way to settle an argument was to find the flaw in one side, to dichotomize the world into the study that was wrong and the study that was right, and now neither side seemed obliging enough to be wrong.

Loick came over at four with his backpack and an agenda of his own. He wanted the spare sleeping bag in the garage because his cousin was visiting and his house was, in his phrasing, at maximum capacity, which meant his cousin had claimed the bed and the couch and, apparently, the floor near the window. He also wanted Colton's opinion on whether asking Katelynn to the winter formal over text was cowardly or merely efficient, a question he raised every twenty minutes the way other people check their phones.

"Text," Colton said, not looking up. "You've been debating this since October. The medium isn't your problem."

"The medium is exactly my problem." Loick dug through the garage and came back with the sleeping bag under one arm and a bag of chips from somewhere. He dropped into the chair across from the two articles. "What is all this?"

"Two studies that disagree about school start times. I'm supposed to compare them and I can't, because they're both fine. They measured slightly different kids and got different answers."

"That sounds like a you problem."

"It's an everyone problem." Colton tapped the red folder, then the blue. "One says move the start time later and kids sleep more. One says it barely matters. If I pick a side, I'm just picking the one I liked first, which is what Mr. Bighorn said not to do." He said this part with a certain bitterness, since being told not to do the easy thing felt like being handed a map with the roads removed.

Loick, chewing, looked at the papers with the mild suspicion of a man examining paperwork he had not signed. "So read a third one."

"That's not how it works. A third one just votes. Then it's two against one and I still don't know anything." But even as he said it, something about the sentence snagged on him. Two against one. Studies weren't votes, but they weren't nothing either, and he wondered, in the loose way he wondered about things before they became useful, whether anyone had ever gathered up all the studies on one question and done something with the pile. Not voted. Pooled. He turned back to the laptop and typed, without much hope, the start times question plus the word he'd seen once in a footnote of the red article and never looked up.

The search result page loaded, and there it was, a 2020 paper with a forest plot that looked like a city skyline lying on its side. He clicked. The word he'd half-remembered sat in the title: a meta-analysis. He read the abstract twice, and the second time through, something in his chest did a small, somatic thing, a loosening he could feel in his shoulders before he could articulate anything in words. A meta-analysis, the paper said in its opening lines, combined the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study could.

"Wait," he said aloud. "Wait, wait."

"You found the answer to your life?"

"Kind of." He was already scrolling. The paper had gathered dozens of studies, both of his among them, and across all of them together the effect was there.
