The gym at the community center smelled like floor wax and old popcorn, and Mia had learned to love both, which was probably a sign of how far gone she was. Saturday was the playoff game against the team from Riverside, and Thursday's practice was the last one before it. She was dribbling through cones when Chase called out from the sideline, holding the ball like evidence.

"Addison's got the hot hand," he said. "Three in a row, in the corner. We run everything through her Saturday."

Addison, at the far basket, sank a fourth and grinned. Mia kept dribbling. She had watched Chase do this before, in the rec league and now here, organizing the offense around whoever had just scored, as if the last shot reached forward and improved the next one. It worked often enough that nobody questioned it. But Mia had spent Sunday at the community center's study room, killing time before her mother's shift ended, and had found a photocopy of a study someone had left in the recycling bin. 1985, by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky. It followed actual shooters through actual seasons and concluded that streaks of makes were no more common than chance would produce. The paper called the "hot hand" a fallacy.

"It's not real," she said now, catching Chase's pass and stopping it dead under her palm. "Three in a row means nothing about the fourth."

"Her fourth just went in."

"Three made shots don't make a fourth more likely. Somebody studied it. Real games, real shooters. The streaks showed up exactly as often as chance."

Chase looked at her the way people look at you when you've insulted their religion by accident. Addison walked over, towel around her neck, and stood beside him, which Mia registered as a kind of alignment. "So we should ignore who's shooting well?" Addison said. "That's your plan for Saturday?"

Mia had spent two days trying to compartmentalize it, the statistics on one shelf, the game she actually played on another, because in her experience they had never argued before. Chance said Addison's streak was noise. The scoreboard said the ball went in. She didn't have a way yet to hold both, and the honest answer was that she wasn't sure the study had ever met a defender like the one Riverside would put on Addison's corner.

"Run the drill," the coach called, and the conversation shattered into footwork. But at water break Chase came back, quiet. "My brother says that too. The fallacy thing. He read it in college."

"Then why'd you argue?"

"Because it's the playoffs, and I'd rather believe in something."

That, Mia thought, was the tangential kind of logic you could actually respect: not evidence, just loyalty, aimed sideways at the truth. She didn't answer, and the detente between them lasted through the rest of practice, polite passes, no eye contact, both of them saving it for Saturday.

In the fourth quarter on Saturday they were down four with two minutes left. Addison had made five in the first half and then gone cold for the whole third, and Chase had kept forcing it to her anyway, because the first half was the story he was telling himself. Mia waved him off at the top of the key, took the screen, and pulled up for the jumper she'd been practicing since October, the one nobody counted as a streak because nobody had made it three times in a row yet. It went in.

Riverside scored, then Chase drove and got fouled. At the line, one for two. Down two, forty seconds. In the huddle, Addison didn't wait for Chase. "Give it to Mia," she said. "She's the one making them."

"Which means nothing about the next one," Mia said.

"Then it doesn't matter who shoots. So give it to you."

Mia laughed once, short, before the whistle cut it off. The inbounds pass came to her at the wing, the defender closing, Chase open at the top calling her name, and she rose into her shot with the whole gym holding its breath.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Social loafing, the drop in effort people make in groups, shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified.
story:
Samuel's backyard was narrow and hedged on two sides, just wide enough for a goal made of two fishing nets lashed to fence posts with binder twine. That was where the whole trouble started, on a Tuesday in late August, when Dimitri brought a stopwatch he had borrowed from his older brother and said they should find out who was actually fast.

The trouble was not the stopwatch. The trouble was that in two weeks Samuel had tryouts for the county team, his first season playing anywhere above the school league, and he had begun to suspect something about himself that he did not like. In practice scrimmages he ran hard. In sprints, lined up with eight other boys, he ran hard too, but not as hard, and the difference lived somewhere he couldn't see.

"Four point one two," Dimitri called out, thumb on the button, spitting sunflower seeds into the flowerbed. "Brendon, you're next. Go."

Brendon went. He was a thick-wristed boy who played defence and claimed he hated running, and he churned down the grass in 4.35, which was better than his usual. They ran again. Samuel ran 4.09, then 4.04, then, on the fourth sprint of the afternoon, when Dimitri read his time aloud before he had even crossed the line, 3.98. He had never broken four seconds in his life.

They lay in the shade of the hedge afterward, passing a water bottle back and forth. "Why is it," Samuel said, "that I run faster when you say my number out loud than I do at practice? Same legs. Same grass, basically."

Dimitri shrugged in that way he had, one shoulder, as though the question were only half interesting. "At practice nobody knows whose time is whose. You finish in a clump."

Samuel turned that over. It sounded true, but sounding true and being true were different animals, and he had learned from Mr. Sánchez, his history teacher, to distrust the argument that arrived too conveniently. Still, the stopwatch had given him something practice never had: a number with his name on it. When the number was his, he could not hide inside the clump. When it was nobody's, apparently, some part of him quietly decided that nobody would notice a half-second of laziness.

He tried to find words for it. "My dad took a psychology course once," he said. "He said there's a thing called social loafing. The drop in effort people make in groups."

"In bread?"

"Loafing, idiot. Like slacking."

"You're saying we slack in groups."

"I'm saying I slack in groups." Samuel said it plainly, because it seemed important to say it plainly, and Brendon, who had been picking at a clover, looked over with something like relief.

"Finally," Brendon said. "I thought it was just me."

The next week, Samuel asked the county coach, a heavy man who coached from a folding chair, whether the team tracked individual sprint times. The coach said the club had a sheet somewhere, from two seasons ago, but nobody had filled it in since. Samuel volunteered to bring a stopwatch. He did not say why. He had a theory about why, but a theory was only a guess wearing better clothes, and he did not want to exculpate himself in advance if the numbers came back and showed that he was, in fact, the slow one all along. He wanted the evidence before the verdict.

So for three practices he stood at the touchline with the borrowed stopwatch, calling out names and numbers, writing both on a clipboard, and something happened that he could watch happening: boys who jogged the fitness runs began to run them. A winger named only by his surname went eleven seconds faster over the lap the first day his own time went on the sheet. By Thursday nobody asked whether they had to be timed. They asked whether they could go again.

On Friday Mr. Sánchez, who lived two doors down and cut through the alley to avoid the traffic on the main road, stopped at the fence while Samuel was collecting the nets. Samuel told him about the stopwatch, about the times, about the clump. He expected the teacher to nod and hand him some framework, the way he did in class, the way teachers did.

Instead Mr. Sánchez said, "And what did you learn about yourself?"

"That I'm faster than I thought and lazier than I thought," Samuel said. "Both at once."

"Most things are both at once," Mr. Sánchez said, and continued down the alley, and Samuel stood holding the wet nets, unsatisfied. It was a comfortable sentence, the kind that could exculpate anyone, and he didn't want comfort. He wanted to know whether the effort would hold once the season started and the clipboard went away. Whether he had found something real about people or only something real about being watched. His brother would have called it a question of epistemology, which was a word Samuel found useless half the time, but here it seemed almost germane: how would he know, and what would count as knowing?

He didn't have an answer, and he was honest enough with himself to leave the question open rather than close it with something tidy.

Dimitri and Brendon came over Saturday morning, uninvited, the way they did. Dimitri had the stopwatch. Brendon had a bag of rolls from the bakery his mother worked at, still warm, and they ate them sitting on the overturned wheelbarrow while the dew burned off the grass.

"One more," Dimitri said, standing, tucking the seeds in his pocket. "For the sheet."

"There's no sheet," Samuel said. "Season hasn't started."

"There's a sheet if you make one."

Samuel looked at the fishing-net goal, at the hedge, at the long wet lane of grass between them, and went inside for the clipboard.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the first derivative test, a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum, because the function rises and then falls.
story:
The math club met on Thursdays in a room that smelled of whiteboard marker and the custodian's coffee, and Michael arrived that day carrying a napkin that had already been through a lot. On it, in his grandfather's shaky ballpoint, was a sign chart: a number line with plus signs to the left of zero and minus signs to the right, and above it, the words "they rise and then they fall." His grandfather had drawn it at the kitchen table on Sunday to settle an argument about whether a rain barrel, filling and then draining, ever held the most water at a single identifiable moment. Michael had lost the argument, and the napkin had won it, and he still didn't fully understand why.

The regional competition was Saturday. Three days. Ms. Barrett had posted the topics on the door in her tidy block letters, and there, third from the top, between "factor theorem" and "optimization word problems," was the thing he couldn't do: derivatives of polynomials. He could differentiate in a mechanical way, dragging the exponent down and subtracting one, but the club's practice problems asked where a quantity peaked, and Michael kept guessing.

He sat down across from Vincent, who was eating a granola bar with the composure of someone who had already finished the problem set. Mariane was at the whiteboard drawing the club's banner for Saturday, a compass and a snake, for reasons she declined to historicize even when pressed. "It's our third year with the snake," was all she said. "The snake has a record."

"Ask him about the barrel," Mariane said, nodding at Michael without turning around.

"I have a barrel question," Michael admitted. He smoothed the napkin on the table between them. "My grandfather says there's a moment, one moment, when it holds the most. He drew this."

Vincent leaned over the plus signs and the minus signs. "Where'd he get this?"

"He was a surveyor. He did this with land, with drainage, I don't know. He just drew it."

Vincent pulled the practice sheet toward them. The problem gave a polynomial for the volume of a box cut from a sheet of cardboard, and asked for the dimensions that maximized it. "Okay," he said. "Do the derivative. The dragging-the-exponent-down thing." Michael did it, pencil moving, and they set the derivative equal to zero and got two candidates, one of which was negative and obviously useless, and one of which was a perfectly respectable fraction.

"So that's it," Michael said. "That's the answer."

"Is it a maximum, though? The derivative is zero there, but zero could be anything. Flat spot." Vincent tapped the napkin. "Your grandfather's thing. What does this even mean?"

Michael looked at the sign chart for a long moment. Plus on the left, minus on the right. He picked up his pencil and, below the derivative he'd computed, drew his own number line, his own plus and minus signs, testing a value on each side of the fraction. He'd assumed the napkin was sentimental, an old man's shorthand, impermeable to actual mathematics. Now he laid his chart beside his grandfather's and the two of them matched, sign for sign. "It rises and then it falls," he said slowly. "Plus, then minus. So it's a local maximum. That's the word. Local maximum. That's the whole thing, isn't it. Where it goes from positive to negative."

"That's the first derivative test," Vincent said, mouth full. "Congratulations, your grandfather taught you calculus over a rain barrel."

The room had gone quiet in the way it did when Ms. Barrett came in with the registration forms, and she stood at the door holding them like indemnity against every possible disaster, spare pencils, a signed permission slip, a printout of the parking situation. She looked at the napkin, then at Michael's number line, then at Michael. "You found that yourself?" she asked.

"Half myself," Michael said. "The other half is eighty-three years old."

She smiled and moved on to collect Vincent's form, and Michael copied the fraction into his notebook, boxed it, then sat looking at it. Because here was the thing he couldn't shake: the local maximum was only local. Somewhere outside the picture the polynomial went on being a polynomial, rising toward some larger peak he hadn't drawn, or falling forever, and the sign chart on the napkin said nothing about any of that. His grandfather's barrel drained to zero and stayed there, which was a comfort of barrels that polynomials did not share. He wrote "local" and underlined it twice, and then, in the margin, in smaller letters, "but is it enough?"

Mariane uncapped a green marker and held it over the banner. "The snake needs a name," she announced to the room. "By Saturday."

Michael capped his pen. "Barrel," he said.

Mariane considered the snake, its length, its attitude. "Barrel," she agreed, and started drawing the letters.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Many food banks cannot accept home-cooked or opened food, because they cannot check how it was prepared or stored.
story:
The flyer had said food bank, so Mia pictured a warehouse, and it took her a minute to acclimate when Ms. Hamdan led her instead through the lobby of the seniors' residence, past a fish tank and a man asleep in a chair, to a bright room where folding tables held crates of tins and pasta boxes. "We run it out of here twice a month," Ms. Hamdan said, handing her a clipboard. "Many of our clients live one floor up." A boy from Mia's chemistry class, Wayne, was already sorting soup by expiry date, and a girl in a hijab, Reem, was taping a sign to the door. Mia had expected strangers. She had not expected to be the only one who didn't know where the garbage bags were.

Her job for the first hour was simple: greet people, log what they took, be pleasant. Most clients were elderly residents, though a few came in from the street with wheeled carts. A woman named nothing on Mia's clipboard chose a bag of rice with hands that trembled, and Reem quietly carried it to the counter for her so she wouldn't have to ask. Mia watched that and made a note of it, not on the clipboard.

At eleven, a man she recognized from her own street, the one who was always fixing his fence, came in carrying a foil pan held level as an offering. "Lasagna," he said. "For the bank. My wife made too much, and it seemed a shame." He set it down and stood there with his hands open.

Mia reached for the clipboard before she understood there was nothing to write. "That's really kind," she said, and then, because she genuinely didn't know, "Let me just check the process." Behind her, Wayne had gone still, and she could feel it, the way you feel a door close in another room.

Ms. Hamdan came over and turned the problem gently in her hands, the way Mia's mother handled eggs. "I'm so sorry," she said. "Many food banks can't accept home-cooked or opened food, because we can't check how it was prepared or stored." She said it warmly, and she held the pan while she said it, as if it weighed something. "It's nothing about your wife's cooking. It's the rule, and it's the same one everywhere."

The man nodded twice, took the pan back, and stood a moment too long before leaving. Mia logged nothing and thought about the rule for the rest of the hour, in the gaps between clients. She had assumed generosity was the whole point, that kindness operated like water, finding every crack. Instead there was a shape to it, a container, and the container had reasons she couldn't see through. On her street the same man's wife had sent over a casserole when Mia's grandmother died, and nobody had asked how it was stored, and it had been the right thing, the exact right thing. She turned both ideas over like two stones from different beaches.

When the line thinned, she asked Wayne about it. "You looked like you knew," she said.

"My first day, I told someone their peanut butter was fine, and it was opened, and Ms. Hamdan had to call them back," he said. "I felt like a criminal. But then I thought about someone with a compromised immune system upstairs eating something that sat out. The rule isn't chicanery. It's care with fences on it."

Reem, restacking crackers, laughed at the phrase but didn't disagree. "My grandmother says rules like that are parochial," she offered. "Small-minded. Food is food." She shrugged. "But my grandmother also once fed forty people from one pot with no incident, so her evidence is personal."

Mia found she couldn't land on either side cleanly, and, oddly, she didn't mind. Maybe the rule protected people she'd never see the faces of; maybe it turned away a warm pan for a cold can, and both things could be true at once, the way her father's and mother's arguments were both true about the move to the apartment. She liked that Ms. Hamdan had held the lasagna like that, though. Whatever the rule was, it could still be carried carefully.

At closing, the fence man was waiting outside the residence doors, foil pan balanced on the railing. "I brought plates," he said, almost shy. "If your volunteers are hungry, it's not the food bank then, is it. It's just neighbours."

Ms. Hamdan looked at the pan, and then at him, and then, very slowly, she reached for it.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
The kitchen smelled of the onions his mother had left sweating in a pan, and Evan sat at the laptop with the portal open in one tab and the Common App open in another, the way he had for eleven days. The status bar still read "Submitted." He refreshed it anyway. It still read "Submitted."

"You're doing the thing again," Shania said from the doorway. She had come over with her own binder of printouts, because her house had no printer and his mother kept the good one on the counter like a public utility. She set the binder down and pulled a chair over, uninvited, which was the arrangement between them.

"I'm not doing the thing. I'm checking my email."

"You're staring at a page that says the same thing it said this morning." She flipped her binder open to a divider labeled December and slid a printed page toward him. "Look, since you're sitting there anyway. This essay question. 'Describe a circumstance that has shaped you.' What do they even want?"

He read it twice. "Something bad that happened to you that you survived. But you can't make it sound like you're asking for pity."

"So, like, extenuating circumstances."

"Except you have to extenuate it yourself," he said. "Build the frame around it. Dad lost his job sophomore year, and if I write about that, the sentence after it better be about what I did, not what it did to me." He heard himself say it and realized it sounded rehearsed, which meant it was true and he had been practicing it in his head for months.

Shania leaned back and looked at the ceiling. "You know what I keep thinking about? My cousin applied in like 1998 and she told me she typed separate applications. Actual separate ones, mailed in envelopes. Twenty schools, twenty packets." She tapped his Common App tab. "This thing, one form, all these schools. It started in 1975 with fifteen member colleges. Now there's more than a thousand of them."

"Fifteen," Evan said.

"Fifteen. She used to complain about it at every Thanksgiving and I didn't believe her until I looked it up." Shania pulled her own laptop toward her and opened her essay document. "Anyway. I'm just saying, I'm grateful. That's all. I get to write one of these instead of twenty."

He watched her start typing, and it put him in mind of something Mr. Yamamoto had said back in October, at the lab bench by the window. Evan had been grinding a sample too long, and Mr. Yamamoto had stopped beside him and said, "Do you know what graphite and diamond have in common?" Evan had admitted he didn't, not really. "Same element. Both carbon. We call the different forms allotropes. Same material, different arrangement, entirely different properties." Then he'd walked off and left Evan with the mortar, which was Mr. Yamamoto's whole method. Evan had thought about it for weeks afterward, that pressure alone decided which one you got, that there was no changing the carbon after.

But sitting here now, watching Shania's cursor blink while his own status stayed frozen at "Submitted," he wasn't sure that was the right reading. A thousand schools, and one form. The form didn't decide what he was; it was just an arrangement, a shape the same handful of facts could take. And yet the school on the other end of his particular arrangement would read it and form a judgment that felt absolute, diamond-hard, permanent. Both things were true at once and he could not get them to sit together cleanly. Maybe the graphite and the diamond were not opposites. Maybe they were just what the same person looked like from different rooms.

"That's a good intro," he said, reading over Shania's shoulder. "The part about your grandmother's kitchen. Keep that."

"Even though it doesn't answer the prompt yet?"

"Especially because it doesn't. It's inchoate right now, which is fine. It becomes an answer later. That's what a draft is." He turned back to his own screen. The tab was still open. His reflection was faint in the dark margin of the page, the overhead light doubled in the monitor, the onion smell thickening behind him.

"Stop refreshing," Shania said without looking up.

"I refreshed once. Maybe twice." He left his hand on the trackpad anyway, and then the tab blinked, and the status changed. A new line appeared under the word Submitted, small and unadorned: a decision had been posted, and a link followed it. He sat very still. Shania had stopped typing. His mother called something from the hallway about dinner in ten minutes, and Evan moved the cursor onto the link and hovered there.

"Open it," Shania said.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 2011 the OPERA experiment reported neutrinos apparently faster than light; in 2012 the result was traced to a loose fibre-optic cable, and other experiments measured speeds consistent with light.
story:
Edouard got to the physics room early so he could claim the desk by the window, the one with a wobble in its leg that nobody else wanted. He spread out his notebook and his phone, screen up, because today he intended to win. The class debate was on whether one experiment could overturn a century of physics, and Mr. Flores had said, in his flat way, that whoever argued best would get the last word. Edouard's father had told him at breakfast that winning an argument was mostly about holding the louder fact, and Edouard had internalized that idea so completely it felt like posture, something he stood up straighter because of.

Kya slid into the seat beside him and put her phone flat on the desk between them. "Look at this," she said. "It's from 2011. This experiment, OPERA, they measured neutrinos going faster than light. Faster than light, Edouard. The headline says it broke Einstein."

"Send it to me," he said. "That's my whole argument. One result, one crack, and the whole thing comes down."

Adrien turned around from the row in front, chewing the end of a pen. "A headline isn't a result," he said. "My uncle bets on headlines and he lives above a laundromat."

"That's a colloquialism for something," Kya said, "I just don't know what."

The bell rang and Mr. Flores shut the door with his heel. He was carrying a stack of photocopies, slightly crooked, the toner grey on the last pages. He set them on the front bench and said nothing, which for Mr. Flores was a kind of speech. When Edouard raised his hand and read out the headline, faster than light, Einstein wrong, Mr. Flores only said, "Begin, then," and sat on the edge of his desk.

Edouard stood. He had the momentum of the fact itself, the pleasure of it, a particle outrunning the speed limit of the universe. "One measurement," he said, "and everything we were taught is provisional." Adrien countered, clipped, that he'd read somewhere that the thing had fallen apart, but he couldn't say where, and the weakness showed. Edouard pressed it. "You don't have a source. I do." He felt the room tilt toward him. Then Mr. Flores slid the photocopies down the rows without comment, and Edouard found himself holding a page of small print with the word OPERA at the top.

He sat down to read while Adrien kept talking, and the page did what Adrien's memory couldn't. In 2012, it said, the result had been traced to a loose fibre-optic cable. Edouard read the line twice. Other experiments had measured neutrino speeds consistent with light. He looked up and Kya was watching his face, waiting to see which of them the paper had beaten.

That evening he lay on his bed with his laptop on his stomach and typed a message to Kya, because he owed her the argument more than he owed Adrien the concession. "You know the thing you sent me," he wrote. "I used it in class like it was a wrecking ball. It wasn't. The cable was loose. A cable, Kya. The speed of light is still the speed of light, and my big moment was a plug half out of the wall." He hesitated, then kept typing. "But here's what I can't shake. For months, in 2011, good scientists believed they might have seen it. They published anyway. They let everyone look. That's not a failure, that's the machine working. One result isn't a verdict, it's an invitation. I still think one experiment matters, just not the way I said. It matters by being wrong loudly, in public, where other people can check it." He deleted the last sentence, then typed it again.

Her reply came while he was brushing his teeth. "So what's your position, then? You went from wrecking ball to 'it's complicated' in one class period."

He typed back: "My position is that I was wrong and the loose cable was right, and if another faster-than-light result shows up tomorrow, I'll want it replicated before I feel anything about it. Maybe replication is the actual verdict. Maybe I'll still get excited anyway. I'm not sure which part of me wins that fight, and I'm not going to pretend I am."

The next morning Kya was already at the wobbly desk, and she didn't move when he came in. "Sit somewhere else," she said. "That's my seat now." Then she slid her phone across so he could see the screen, a fresh headline about a new anomaly in some detector, and raised one eyebrow at him.

Edouard looked at it for a long moment, then pulled out his notebook and wrote at the top of a clean page, in his careful hand: who else has measured this? He handed the phone back.

"Ask me again in a year," he said.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: North Dakota is the only US state without voter registration; it abolished registration in 1951, and voters instead show identification at the polls.
story:
Nicolas found the envelope from the county elections office on the kitchen counter on a Tuesday afternoon, propped against the fruit bowl like a bill he was meant to pay. Inside was a voter registration form, folded in thirds, with a pen line already drawn through the boxes his mother had filled in for herself. His eighteenth birthday had come and gone three weeks earlier, in the quiet way of March birthdays, and now the state was asking him a question he had not expected to be complicated: was he ready to say, on paper, where he lived and what he believed a ballot was worth.

He carried the form upstairs and set it on his desk beside a half-built model bridge from an engineering elective he had never finished. He was working through the boxes, street address, party affiliation, when his phone lit up with a message from Erica, who had moved in January from North Dakota to the house four doors down. She had sent a photo of her own form and a single line of question marks. Below that: "They're saying I have to register first? That's not a thing. Do I mail this or what?"

Nicolas called her, and she talked fast the way she did when she was embarrassed, explaining that at home there had never been a form, never a deadline, never a clerk. You showed up, you showed your ID, you voted. She had gone with her father every November since she was small and watched him walk in without paperwork, out again in ten minutes, the little sticker on his jacket. Nicolas, who had registered two days ago without thinking, did not believe her at first. It sounded like a family shortcut mistaken for a law.

"Everywhere has registration," he said. "That's the whole point. You can't just walk in."

"I'm telling you," Erica said. "Look it up before you laugh at me."

He opened his laptop while she stayed on the line, and after a few minutes of searching he sat back in his chair. She was right, and more than right: North Dakota was the only state in the country without voter registration. It had abolished registration in 1951, and voters there showed identification at the polls instead. He read the sentence twice, then read it aloud to her, and heard her exhale on the other end, vindicated and still annoyed. The confounder, he realized, was not that her state was strange but that his was, and he had never once noticed. Registration had been presented to him as a law of nature, like gravity, when it was really just a habit his state kept.

There was a flashback then, unbidden, the way memory arrives while your hands are still on a keyboard. Fourth grade, Ms. Bondarenko's classroom, the November after a big election. She had brought in a sample ballot and a mock polling booth made from a cardboard box, and she had made each of them register on an index card before voting on the class pet's name. Nicolas had written his name in careful letters and felt, for the first time, the small exhilaration of being counted. He had assumed the index card was a miniature of something universal. Now he understood it had been a miniature of one arrangement among several, a choice somebody had made and somebody else, in another state, had unmade.

The problem, though, was practical, and Erica still had it. She could not vote here without registering, whatever North Dakota allowed, and the deadline was Friday. Her parents were obdurate about the mail, distrustful of envelopes, and she did not know whether a photocopy of her license counted as identification. So Nicolas did the only thing that seemed useful: he walked four doors down in the thin evening light, form in his jacket pocket, and the two of them filled hers out at her kitchen table while her mother washed dishes and argued pleasantly about where to find a stamp. They solved it in twenty minutes. The form would go out in the morning mail, and by the next election she would be, in this state's eyes, a registered voter.

Walking home, Nicolas turned the whole evening over without settling it. He had started the day certain that voting began with paperwork, and he had learned that it didn't have to, that somewhere in the country a person could simply appear and be believed. Whether that was freedom or risk he could not say, and he found he liked holding both possibilities at once, the way you can admire a bridge and still want to check the bolts. Back at his desk, the model bridge waited, unfinished, its last span not yet glued.

He picked up the pen and, before he could think further, wrote his name on a blank index card and propped it against the bridge.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly.
story:
Clara had spent every Saturday since September in the kennels at the animal shelter, walking dogs whose names she knew better than some classmates', so when Ms. Thompson suggested she add a shift at the food bank next door, she assumed the two would feel similar. They shared a parking lot, the shelter and the food bank, divided by a chain-link gate that someone always left ajar, and on her first morning Clara crossed through it carrying a clipboard and the certainty that before long, people would start arriving for groceries.

The warehouse behind the loading dock was colder than the kennels and smelled of cardboard instead of bleach. Loan, a junior who had volunteered there for a year, was already breaking down flattened boxes with a speed that suggested practice. She waved Clara over and pointed to a pallet of canned beans. "We sort, we box, we load," she said. "Pantry orders come in by email, and the van goes out Thursdays."

Clara sorted. The work was simple enough that her mind wandered, and around ten she found herself standing at the open bay door, watching the parking lot. A woman walked up the drive, crossed the asphalt, hesitated at the threshold, and then turned and went back toward the road. Clara set down her clipboard. "Shouldn't there be people coming in?" she asked. "I mean, it's a food bank. Where does everyone get their food?"

Loan laughed, not unkindly, and Jeremiah, who had been taping boxes in the corner and was so reticent that Clara had assumed he didn't speak English, surprised her by answering first. "Nobody shops here," he said. "That's what a food pantry is for." He went back to his tape gun as if he hadn't spoken at all.

Loan took over from there, but in pieces, the way she explained everything, as though she were laying out items on a table. "So the food bank is the warehouse. It collects everything, from the drives and the grocery stores, and then it distributes to the local agencies. The church on Miller Street, the school, the community center. Those are the pantries. That's where people actually pick up the food, directly." She shrugged. "I thought the same thing my first day. I kept waiting for a line."

Clara turned this over while she worked. She had imagined charity as a door people walked through, a counter, a hand passing a bag to a hand. Instead the building she stood in was a kind of lung, taking in and sending out, visible to almost no one it fed. It reminded her of the shelter's back rooms, the intake wing where the public never went, where dogs arrived frightened and were coaxed back toward adoptability before anyone ever saw them. The suffering and the rescue both happened offstage. She wasn't sure whether that hiddenness was a kindness, sparing people the spectacle of their own need, or whether it made it too easy for a town to forget the need existed at all.

The woman who had turned away at the door came back at noon, and this time Clara was the one closest to the bay, so she went out to meet her. "Hi," Clara said. "Are you looking for something?" The woman held her car keys tight in one fist and said, quietly, that she needed groceries but her pantry, the one at the church, was closed until Tuesday, and someone had told her to try here. Clara felt the shape of the mistake before she knew how to correct it. "This is the warehouse," she said. "We send the food out to the pantries. We can't actually give it to you here." The words felt wrong even as she said them, like refusing someone water while standing in a reservoir.

Inside, Ms. Thompson had come over from the shelter side with a crate of blankets for the cold-weather drive, and she had heard enough through the open door. She didn't intervene with the woman directly, but she caught Clara's eye and nodded toward the office, where Loan was already printing something. It turned out to be the schedule for every pantry in the county, hours and addresses, and Loan handed it to Clara to carry back out. Clara walked it to the parking lot, explained the hours at the elementary school, which was open Saturday afternoons, and the woman thanked her twice, still holding her keys, and drove away.

Afterward Clara stacked canned beans until her shoulders ached, and she thought about the way the whole system, invisible and orderly, had both failed that woman this morning and worked for her by the afternoon. Maybe the design was right and the signage was wrong; maybe the hiddenness was a flaw she had only noticed because she'd been the one standing in the doorway. She didn't have it settled, and she found she didn't mind that. She had come wanting to hand bags to people, and instead she had learned the architecture of the thing, the warehouse and the pantry, the lung and the door. When the Thursday van pulled in early, Loan tossed her a box cutter without a word, and Clara caught it and got to work.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
The food bank had set up its tables in the common room of the seniors' residence because the church basement flooded, and so Kaylee spent her first morning volunteering between a card table stacked with tins and a wall of faded photographs of dance recitals from 1987. She had come because her school required forty hours of service, which she had planned to metabolize the way she metabolized most obligations, quickly and without indigestion. Gianluca had signed up beside her on the same form, and Kylie had come only because Gianluca came, and the three of them stood at nine in the morning holding clipboards they did not yet know how to use.

The line, when it formed, went down the corridor and out through the lobby and past the bus shelter on River Street. Kylie counted heads twice, moving her lips, and then said, "It's a Tuesday. A weekday morning. Where do all these people even come from on a Tuesday?" She said it quietly, but not quietly enough, and a woman in a grey coat three places back looked at her shoes.

Mr. Ma, who lived on the second floor and had appointed himself the unofficial greeter of anything that happened in his building, sat by the door with a thermos. He did not explain the line. He said, "You'll want the pasta on the lower shelf, it's heavier than it looks," and, to a man with a walker, "There's a chair here with your name on it," and he was right, because he had taped a strip of paper reading HAROLD to the armrest an hour earlier.

A man in a delivery jacket, still holding his keys, told Kaylee he had twenty minutes before his shift and could not wait for the produce table to open. She wanted to tell him that the rules were the rules, that everyone had somewhere to be, and instead she found herself walking the length of the line asking who was on a break from work, who had a bus to catch, who had children waiting. It felt like cheating. It also felt like the only thing worth doing, and she could not make those two feelings sit still next to each other.

Gianluca, unpacking a crate of dented soup, said he had read something on the drive over. "My mom had the radio on. Food Banks Canada does this count, HungerCount, and in March of this year it was nearly 2.2 million visits in one month. In Canada. That's a record for a single month." He said it the way he reported everything, flat, as if the numbers would speak for themselves, and then he went quiet, because the numbers had, in fact, spoken, and the line was still visible through the lobby glass, and nobody had anything to add.

Kaylee worked the problem in her head while she bagged rice. She had always thought of volunteering as a kind of asymptote, a curve you drew in math class that got closer and closer to the line of actually fixing something without ever touching it, and she had been fine with that, comfortable even, because the nearness was the point. But two point two million in a month was not a shape on a graph. It was this corridor, this Tuesday, the woman in the grey coat who had taken one tin of tomatoes and put it back, saying she should leave some for others.

At noon the crowd thinned and Kylie sat down hard on a folding chair. "I thought it would feel good," she said. "It feels like bailing water." Mr. Ma poured tea from his thermos into the thermos lid, which was a cup, and offered it to her, and she took it, and he said, "Harold plays chess on Thursdays if you're short of people to lose to," which was not an answer to anything she had said and was somehow, exactly, an answer.

There had been one moment Kaylee kept returning to. A boy from her school, Dev, from two grades below, had come through the line with his grandmother, and Kaylee had handed him the bag and he had looked at her for a half second with a face that said, please, don't, and she had turned to the clipboard instead and called the next number. She could not decide whether that had been kindness or cowardice. She suspected it was both, and she suspected that most of what she would do in her life would be both, and that this was not a reason to stop.

Gianluca drove them home with the windows cracked. "Same time next week?" he said, and Kylie, who had sworn in the car that morning that she was never waking up at eight on a Saturday again, looked out the window and said, "I'll think about it," which Kaylee recognized, from long experience, as a yes. She texted her mother that she would be late for dinner, then deleted the text, then sent it anyway. In the cup holder, Mr. Ma's thermos lid, which Kylie had washed and forgotten to return, sat cooling in the sun.
